newsitem.title: CHINA: Vietnam's Do Muoi in China for visit.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam's Do Muoi in China for visit.

text.p: Vietnam's Communist Party General Secretary Do Muoi arrived in Beijing on Monday for a five-day visit in the wake of a dispute over Chinese oil drilling in contested waters of the South China Sea.

Jiang Zemin, general secretary of China's Communist Party, held a welcoming ceremony for Muoi followed by talks at Beijing's Great Hall of the People, the official Xinhua news agency said. It did not give details of the talks.
Muoi was quoted by Xinhua as saying on arrival that his visit was "very important ... and aimed at consolidating and developing Sino-Vietnamese friendly cooperative relations".
Jiang, who is also state president and chief of China's military, was scheduled to hold a state banquet in Muoi's honour in the evening, a spokesman for Hanoi's embassy in Beijing said.

China and Vietnam traded accusations over Beijing's decision to move the Kan Tan III rig, owned by China's National Offshore Oil Corp, into an area roughly midway between the coast of central Vietnam and China's southern Hainan island in March.
Although the rig was withdrawn, subsequent talks in Beijing aimed at preventing a recurrence failed to find common ground.
Muoi will meet other Chinese leaders on Tuesday, including Premier Li Peng, Qiao Shi, head of China's parliament, and Li Ruihuan, head of an advisory body to parliament, Chinese officials said.
The 80-year-old chief of Vietnam's Communist Party is visiting China at Jiang's invitation and will leave on July 18.
China and Vietnam have a long history of animosity and distrust despite their ideological similarities.
Chinese forces invaded in 1979 to punish Hanoi for its invasion of Cambodia. The brief but savage war that ensued cost at least 20,000 lives.
Tension over competing claims to sovereignty over the potentially oil-rich Paracel and Spratly islands has bubbled beneath the surface despite normalisation of relations in 1991.
In 1994, the two sides agreed to set up a group of experts to discuss their problems in the South China Sea.

Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and China's rival, Taiwan, have also staked claims to all or part of the scattered and barren Spratlys that straddle strategic sea lanes. China has occupied the Paracels since 1974.
An exchange of visits between Chinese and Vietnamese leaders in recent years have led to warmer bilateral relations.
Premier Li visited Vietnam in July last year.
Muoi last visited China in November 1995, four years after the two countries normalised diplomatic ties.
Vietnam refused to mourn the death in February of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, the man seen as being responsible for the 1979 Sino-Vietnamese border war.
